{{Short description|Mathematical result}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma''' is a result named after [[William B. Johnson (mathematician)|William B. Johnson]] and [[Joram Lindenstrauss]] concerning low-distortion [[embedding]]s of points from high-dimensional into low-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. The [[Lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] states that a set of points in a high-dimensional space can be embedded into a space of much lower dimension in such a way that distances between the points are [[Stretch factor|nearly preserved]]. In the classical proof of the lemma, the embedding is a [[random]] [[orthogonal projection]].

The lemma has applications in [[compressed sensing]], [[manifold learning]], [[dimensionality reduction]],  [[graph embedding]], and [[natural language processing]]. Much of the data stored and manipulated on computers, including text and images, can be represented as points in a high-dimensional space (see [[vector space model]] for the case of text). However, the essential algorithms for working with such data tend to become bogged down very quickly as dimension increases. {{#tag:ref|For instance, writing about [[nearest neighbor search]] in high-dimensional data sets, [[Jon Kleinberg]] writes: "The more sophisticated algorithms typically achieve a query time that is logarithmic in ''n'' at the expense of an exponential dependence on the dimension ''d''; indeed, even the average case analysis of heuristics such as k-d trees reveal an exponential dependence on ''d'' in the query time. <ref>{{citation
 | last = Kleinberg | first = Jon M.|author-link=Jon Kleinberg
 | contribution = Two Algorithms for Nearest-neighbor Search in High Dimensions
 | doi = 10.1145/258533.258653
 | isbn = 0-89791-888-6
 | location = New York, NY, USA
 | pages = 599–608
 | publisher = ACM
 | series = STOC '97
 | title = Proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing
 | year = 1997| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>|group=Note}}  It is therefore desirable to reduce the dimensionality of the data in a way that preserves its relevant structure.  

== Statement ==
Given <math>0 < \varepsilon < 1</math>, a set <math>X</math> of <math>N</math> points in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> , and an integer <math>k > 8(\ln N)/\varepsilon^2</math>,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fernandez-Granda |first1=Carlos |title=Lecture notes 5: Random projections |url=https://cims.nyu.edu/~cfgranda/pages/OBDA_spring16/material/random_projections.pdf |page=6 |quote=Lemma 2.6 (Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma)}}</ref> there is a [[linear map]] <math>f: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k</math> such that

: <math>(1-\varepsilon)\|u-v\|^2 \leq \|f(u) - f(v)\|^2 \leq (1+\varepsilon)\|u-v\|^2</math>

for all <math>u,v \in X</math>.

The formula can be rearranged:<math display="block">(1+\varepsilon)^{-1}\|f(u)-f(v)\|^2 \leq \|u-v\|^2 \leq (1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\|f(u)-f(v)\|^2 </math>

Alternatively, for any <math>\varepsilon\in(0,1)</math> and any integer <math>k\ge15(\ln N)/\varepsilon^2</math><ref group=Note>Or any integer <math>k>128(\ln N)/(9\varepsilon^2).</math></ref> there exists a linear function <math>f: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k</math> such that the restriction <math>f|_X</math> is <math>(1+\varepsilon)</math>-[[Lipschitz continuity#Definition|bi-Lipschitz]].<ref group=Note>This result follows from the above result. Sketch of proof: Note <math>1/(1+\varepsilon)<\sqrt{1-3\varepsilon/4}</math> and <math>\sqrt{1+3\varepsilon/4}<\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}<1+\varepsilon</math> for all <math>\varepsilon\in(0,1)</math>. Do casework for 1=''N'' and 1<''N'', applying the above result to <math>3\varepsilon/4</math> in the latter case, noting <math>128/9<15.</math></ref>

Also, the lemma is tight up to a constant factor, i.e. there exists a set of points of size ''N'' that needs dimension

:<math> \Omega \left(\frac{\log(N)}{\varepsilon^2}\right)</math>

in order to preserve the distances between all pairs of points within a factor of <math>(1 \pm \varepsilon)</math>.<ref>
{{citation
 | contribution=Optimality of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma
 | title=Proceedings of the 58th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
 | year=2017
 | doi=10.1109/FOCS.2017.64
 | first1=Kasper Green|last1= Larsen|author1-link=Kasper Green Larsen
 | first2=Jelani|last2= Nelson|author2-link=Jelani Nelson
 | pages=633–638
 | arxiv=1609.02094
 | isbn=978-1-5386-3464-6
 | s2cid=16745
 }}
</ref>

The classical proof of the lemma takes <math>f</math> to be a scalar multiple of an orthogonal projection <math>P</math> onto a random subspace of dimension <math>k</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. An orthogonal projection collapses some dimensions of the space it is applied to, which reduces the length of all vectors, as well as distance between vectors in the space. Under the conditions of the lemma, [[concentration of measure]] ensures there is a nonzero chance that a random orthogonal projection reduces pairwise distances between all points in <math>X</math> by roughly a constant factor <math>c</math>. Since the chance is nonzero, such projections must exist, so we can choose one <math>P</math> and set <math>f(v) = Pv/c</math>.

To obtain the projection algorithmically, it suffices [[with high probability]] to repeatedly sample orthogonal projection matrices at random. If you keep rolling the dice, you will eventually obtain one in polynomial random time.

== Proof ==
The proof below is based on the course notes of Afonso Bandeira that can be found at the following link.<ref>[https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-s096-topics-in-mathematics-of-data-science-fall-2015/f9261308512f6b90e284599f94055bb4_MIT18_S096F15_Ses15_16.pdf MIT 18.S096 (Fall 2015): Topics in Mathematics of Data Science, Lecture 5, Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma and Gordons Theorem]</ref>

Construct a [[random matrix]] <math>A \sim \mathcal N(0,1)^{k \times n}
</math>, obtained by sampling each entry from the standard [[normal distribution]]. Define <math display=inline>P := \frac{A}{\sqrt k}
</math>, then for any nonzero vector <math>x \in \R^n
</math>, let the projected vector be <math>\hat x := A x 
</math>. Standard geometric arguments show that <math display=inline>r := \frac{\|\hat x\|^2}{\| x\|^2}
</math> is [[Chi-squared distribution|chi-square distributed]], that is, <math display=inline>r \sim \chi^2(k)
</math>. Thus, it satisfies a [[Chi-squared distribution#Concentration|concentration inequality for the chi-squared distribution]]:<math display="block">\Pr(r \in (1\pm \epsilon ) k ) \geq 1 - 2e^{-\frac k2 \left(\frac 12 \epsilon^2 - \frac 13 \epsilon^3\right)}</math>

By the union bound, the probability that this relation is true for all of <math>x_1, \dots, x_N</math> is greater than <math display=inline>1 - 2N e^{-\frac k2 (\frac 12 \epsilon^2 - \frac 13 \epsilon^3)}</math>.

When <math display=inline>k \geq \frac{4\ln 2N}{\epsilon^2\left(1 - 2\epsilon / 3\right)}</math>, the probability is nonzero.

More generally, when <math display=inline>k \geq \frac{4(d+1)\ln 2N}{\epsilon^2\left(1 - \frac{2\epsilon}{3}\right)}</math>, the probability is greater than, or equal to <math display=inline>1 - \frac{1}{(2N)^d} </math>, allowing arbitrarily high probability of success per sample, and ''a fortiori'' polynomial random time.

== Alternate statement ==
A related lemma is the distributional JL lemma. This lemma states that for any <math> 0 < \varepsilon, \delta < 1/2 </math> and positive integer <math> d </math>, there exists a distribution over <math> \mathbb{R}^{k \times d} </math> from which the matrix <math> A </math> is drawn such that for <math> k = O(\varepsilon^{-2} \log(1/\delta)) </math> and for any unit-length  vector <math> x \in \mathbb{R}^{d} </math>, the claim below holds.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Johnson
 | first1 = William B.
 | author1-link = William B. Johnson (mathematician)
 | last2 = Lindenstrauss
 | first2 = Joram
 | author2-link = Joram Lindenstrauss
 | contribution = Extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space
 | doi = 10.1090/conm/026/737400
 | location = Providence, RI
 | mr = 737400
 | pages = [https://archive.org/details/conferenceinmode0000conf/page/189 189–206]
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | series = Contemporary Mathematics
 | title = Conference in modern analysis and probability (New Haven, Conn., 1982)
 | volume = 26
 | year = 1984
 | editor1-last = Beals
 | editor1-first = Richard
 | editor2-last = Beck
 | editor2-first = Anatole
 | editor3-last = Bellow
 | editor3-first = Alexandra
 | display-editors = 3
 | editor4-last = Hajian
 | editor4-first = Arshag
 | isbn = 0-8218-5030-X
 | s2cid = 117819162
 | url-access = registration
 | url = https://archive.org/details/conferenceinmode0000conf/page/189
 }}
</ref>
: <math> P(|\Vert Ax\Vert_2^2-1|>\varepsilon)<\delta</math>

One can obtain the JL lemma from the distributional version by setting <math>x = (u-v)/\|u-v\|_2</math> and <math>\delta < 1/n^2</math> for some pair ''u'',''v'' both in ''X''. Then the JL lemma follows by a union bound over all such pairs.

== Sparse JL transform ==

=== Database-friendly JL transform ===
(Achlioptas, 2003)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Achlioptas |first=Dimitris |date=June 2003 |title=Database-friendly random projections: Johnson-Lindenstrauss with binary coins |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-0000(03)00025-4 |journal=Journal of Computer and System Sciences |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=671–687 |doi=10.1016/s0022-0000(03)00025-4 |issn=0022-0000|url-access=subscription }}</ref> proposed "database-friendly" JL transform, using matrices with only entries from (-1, 0, +1).

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=Achlioptas, 2003, Theorem 1.1|math_statement= 

Let the random <math display="inline">k \times n</math> projection matrix <math display="inline">R</math> have entries drawn i.i.d., either from

<math display="block">
 R_{i j}= \begin{cases}+1 & \text { with probability } 1 / 2 \\ -1 & \text { with probability } 1 / 2\end{cases}
 </math>

or from <math display="block">
 R_{i j}= \begin{cases}+\sqrt{3} & \text { with probability } 1 / 6 \\ 0 & \text { with probability } 2/3 \\ -\sqrt{3} & \text { with probability } 1 / 6 \end{cases}
 </math>

Given a vector <math display="inline">v</math>, we define the random projection <math display="inline">f(v)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}} R v</math>. Then for any vector <math display="inline">v\in \R^n</math>, we have <math display="block">
 \begin{aligned}
 &-\ln Pr(\|f(v)\|_2^2 \geq (1+\epsilon) \|v\|_2^2) \geq \frac k2 \left(\frac{\epsilon^2}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^3}{3} \right) \quad &\forall \epsilon > 0 \\
 &-\ln Pr(\|f(v)\|_2^2 \leq (1-\epsilon) \|v\|_2^2) \geq \frac k2 \left(\frac{\epsilon^2}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^3}{3} \right) \quad &\forall \epsilon \in (0, 1)
 \end{aligned}
 </math>
}}

Fix some [[unit vector]] <math display="inline">v \in \R^n</math>. Define <math display="inline">Q_i := \sum_j R_{ij} v_j</math>. We have <math display="inline"> \|f(v)\|_2^2 = \frac{1}{k} \sum_i Q_i^2 </math>.

Now, since the <math display="inline">Q_1, \dots, Q_k</math> are IID, we want to apply a Chernoff concentration bound for <math display="inline">\frac 1k \sum_i Q_i^2</math> around 1. This requires upper-bounding the [[cumulant generating function]] (CGF).

{{Math theorem|name=Moment bounds|note=Achlioptas, 2003, Section 6|math_statement= 

For any <math display="inline">k \in 1, 2, \dots</math>, the moment of <math display="inline">Q_i</math> is upper-bound by the standard gaussian <math display="inline">Z \sim N(0, 1)</math>:
<math display="block">
 E[Q_i^{2k-1}] = 0 = E[Z^{2k-1}], \quad E[Q_i^{2k}] \leq E[Z^{2k}]
 </math>

}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

<math display="inline">E[Q_i^{2k-1}] = 0</math> is easy: just apply the fact that <math display="inline">E[R_{ij_1}\dots R_{ij_l}] = 0</math> when <math display="inline">l</math> is odd, since we can decompose it into a product of expectations, and one of those is the expectation of an odd power of Radamacher, which is zero.

Now, the trick is that we can rewrite <math display="inline">Z</math> as <math display="inline">Z = \sum_i Z_iv_i</math>, where each <math display="inline">Z_1, \dots, Z_d</math> is a standard gaussian. Then we need to compare: <math display="block">
      E[Q_i^{2k}] = \sum_{j_1, j_2, \dots, j_{2k-1}, j_{2k}}E[R_{ij_1}R_{ij_2}\dots R_{ij_{2k-1}}R_{ij_{2k}}] v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}
      </math> and<br />
<math display="block">
      E[Z^{2k}] = \sum_{j_1, j_2, \dots, j_{2k-1}, j_{2k}}E[Z_{j_1}Z_{j_2}\dots Z_{j_{2k-1}}Z_{j_{2k}}] v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}
      </math> 

In the top sum, a term <math display="block">E[R_{ij_1}R_{ij_2}\dots R_{ij_{2k-1}}R_{ij_{2k}}] v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}</math> decomposes into a product of expectations, times <math display="inline">v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}</math>. The product of expectations is zero, unless the indices <math display="inline">j_1, j_2, \dots, j_{2k}</math> are paired off. In that case, the term <math display="inline">v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}</math> is the square of something, and so<br />
<math display="block">v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}} \geq 0</math> while <math display="inline">R_{ij_1}R_{ij_2}\dots R_{ij_{2k-1}}R_{ij_{2k}}</math> is also the square of <math display="inline">\pm 1</math>, and so<br />
<math display="block">
      E[R_{ij_1}R_{ij_2}\dots R_{ij_{2k-1}}R_{ij_{2k}}] = 1
      </math> 

In the bottom sum, we run a similar argument with each such term <math display="block">E[Z_{j_1}Z_{j_2}\dots Z_{j_{2k-1}}Z_{j_{2k}}] v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}</math> but in this case, since we have <math display="inline">E[Z^{2k}] = (2k-1)!! \geq 1</math>, we find that in each case,<br />
<math display="block">
      E[R_{ij_1}R_{ij_2}\dots R_{ij_{2k-1}}R_{ij_{2k}}] v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}} \leq 
      E[Z_{j_1}Z_{j_2}\dots Z_{j_{2k-1}}Z_{j_{2k}}] v_{j_1}v_{j_2}\dots v_{j_{2k-1}}v_{j_{2k}}
      </math>

And so, summing all of them up, <math display="inline">E[Q_i^{2k}] \leq E[Z^{2k}]</math>.

The same argument works for the other case. Specifically, if <math display="inline">R_{ij}</math> is distributed like that, then <math display="inline">E[R_{ij}^{2k}] =3^{k-1}\leq (2k-1)!!</math>, and the proof goes through exactly the same way.

}}{{hidden end}}

Now that <math display="inline">Q_i</math> is stochastically dominated by the standard gaussian, and <math display="inline">E[Q_i^2] = 1</math>, it remains to perform a [[Chernoff bound]] for <math display="inline">Q_i^2</math>, which requires bounding the cumulant generating function on both ends.

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=The rest of the calculation}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=

For any <math display="inline">t \in (0, 1/2)</math>, we can compute the cumulant generating function <math display="block">
 \begin{aligned}
 K_{Q_i^2}(t) &= \ln E[e^{Q_i^2t}] \\
 &= \ln\sum_k \frac{t^k}{k!}E[Q_i^{2k}] \\
 &\leq \ln\left( 1 + \sum_k \frac{t^k}{k!}(2k-1)!!\right) \\
 &= -\frac 12 \ln(1-2t)
 \end{aligned}
 </math>

Similarly, for any <math display="inline">t\in (0, k/2)</math>, <math display="block">K_{\frac 1k \sum_i Q_i^2}(t) = \sum_i K_{ Q_i^2}(t/k) \leq -\frac k2 \ln(1-2t/k)</math>

So by the standard Chernoff bound method, for any <math display="inline">t \in (0, k/2)</math> and any <math display="inline">\epsilon > 0</math>, <math display="block">
 -\ln Pr\left(\frac 1k \sum_i Q_i^2 \geq 1+\epsilon\right) \geq (1+\epsilon)t + \frac k2 \ln(1-2t/k)
 </math>

The right side is maximized at <math display="inline">t = \frac{k\epsilon}{2(1+\epsilon)}</math>, at which point we have <math display="block">
 -\ln Pr\left(\frac 1k \sum_i Q_i^2 \geq 1 + \epsilon \right) \geq \frac k2 (\epsilon - \ln(1+\epsilon)) \geq \frac k2 (\epsilon^2/2 - \epsilon^3/3)
 </math>

That’s one half of the bound done. For the other half, begin with some <math display="inline">t > 0</math>, and expand the exponential to the second order: <math display="block">
 \begin{aligned}
 K_{Q_i^2}(-t) &= \ln E[e^{-Q_i^2t}] \\
 &\leq \ln E[1-Q_i^2t + Q_i^4t^2/2] \\
 &\leq \ln (1 - t + 3t^2/2)\\
 \end{aligned}
 </math>

<math display="block">K_{\frac 1k \sum_i Q_i^2}(-t) \leq k\ln (1 - t/k + 3t^2/(2k^2))</math>

So by the standard Chernoff bound method, for any <math display="inline">t > 0</math> and any <math display="inline">\epsilon \in (0, 1)</math>, <math display="block">
 -\ln Pr\left(\frac 1k \sum_i Q_i^2 \leq 1 - \epsilon \right) \geq -k[(1-\epsilon)(t/k) + \ln (1 - t/k + 3t^2/(2k^2))]
 </math>

Plug in <math display="inline">t = \frac{k\epsilon}{2(1+\epsilon)}</math>, and simplify, we find the right side is <math display="block">
 \geq k \left(\frac{(\epsilon-1) \epsilon}{2(\epsilon+1)}-\ln\left(\frac{7 \epsilon^2+12 \epsilon+8}{8(\epsilon+1)^2}\right) \right)
 </math> and expand to third Taylor power,<br />
<math display="block">
 \geq k(\epsilon^2/4 - 7\epsilon^3/48) > \frac k2 (\epsilon^2/2 - \epsilon^3/3)
 </math>

}}{{hidden end}}

=== Sparser JL transform on well-spread vectors ===
(Matoušek, 2008)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Matoušek |first=Jiří |author-link=Jiří Matoušek (mathematician) |date=September 2008 |title=On variants of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/rsa.20218 |journal=Random Structures & Algorithms |language=en |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=142–156 |doi=10.1002/rsa.20218 |issn=1042-9832|url-access=subscription }}</ref> proposed a variant of the above JL transform that is even more sparsified, though it only works on "well-spread" vectors.

{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem
| note = Matoušek 2008, Theorem 4.1
| math_statement = Assume that <math display="inline">n \in \N, \epsilon \in (0, 1/2), \delta \in (0, 1), \alpha \in [n^{-1/2}, 1], q \in [C_0 \alpha^2 \ln(n/\epsilon \delta), 1], k \in [C_1 \epsilon^{-2}\ln\frac 4\delta, n]</math>, where <math display="inline">C_0, C_1</math> are absolute constants, and ''k'' is an integer.

Let <math display="inline">R</math> be a <math display="inline">k \times n</math> matrix sampled IID with

<math display="block">
      R_{ij}= \begin{cases}+q^{-1 / 2} & \text { with probability } \frac{1}{2} q \\ -q^{-1 / 2} & \text { with probability } \frac{1}{2} q \\ 0 & \text { with probability } 1-q\end{cases}
      </math>
	  
Then, for any unit vector <math display="inline">v \in \R^n</math> such that <math display="inline">\|v\|_\infty \leq \alpha</math>, we have <math display="block">
      Pr(\|f(v)\|_2^2 \in [1\pm \epsilon] ) \geq 1-\delta
      </math>

where <math>f(v) = \frac{1}{\sqrt k}Rv</math>.
}}The above cases are generalized to the case for matrices with independent, mean-zero, unit variance, [[Sub-Gaussian distribution|subgaussian]] entries in (Dirksen, 2016).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dirksen |first=Sjoerd |date=2016-10-01 |title=Dimensionality Reduction with Subgaussian Matrices: A Unified Theory |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10208-015-9280-x |journal=Foundations of Computational Mathematics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=1367–1396 |doi=10.1007/s10208-015-9280-x |issn=1615-3383|arxiv=1402.3973 }}</ref>

== Speeding up the JL transform ==
Given ''A'', computing the matrix vector product takes <math>O(kd)</math> time. There has been some work in deriving distributions for which the matrix vector product can be computed in less than <math>O(kd)</math> time.

There are two major lines of work. The first, ''Fast Johnson Lindenstrauss Transform'' (FJLT),<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ailon | first1 = Nir | last2 = Chazelle | first2 = Bernard|author2-link=Bernard Chazelle
 | contribution = Approximate nearest neighbors and the fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss transform
 | title = Proceedings of the 38th Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing
 | year = 2006
 | mr = 2277181
 | doi = 10.1145/1132516.1132597
 | pages = 557–563
 | publisher = ACM Press
 | location = New York
 | isbn = 1-59593-134-1| s2cid = 490517 }}
</ref> was introduced by Ailon and [[Bernard Chazelle|Chazelle]] in 2006.
This method allows the computation of the matrix vector product in just <math>d\log d + k^{2+\gamma}</math> for any constant <math>\gamma>0</math>.

Another approach is to build a distribution supported over matrices that are sparse.<ref>{{citation
 | first1 = Daniel M. | last1 = Kane | last2 = Nelson |author1-link=Daniel Kane (mathematician) | first2 = Jelani|author2-link=Jelani Nelson
 | doi = 10.1145/2559902
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 1 | journal = [[Journal of the ACM]]
 | title = Sparser Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transforms
 | volume = 61
 | year = 2014
 | mr = 3167920| arxiv = 1012.1577| s2cid = 7821848 }}. A preliminary version of this paper was published in the ''Proceedings of the Twenty-Third Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms'', 2012.</ref>
This method allows keeping only an <math>\varepsilon</math> fraction of the entries in the matrix, which means the computation can be done in just <math>kd\varepsilon</math> time.
Furthermore, if the vector has only <math>b</math> non-zero entries, the Sparse JL takes time <math>kb\varepsilon</math>, which may be much less than the <math>d\log d</math> time used by Fast JL.

== Tensorized random projections ==
It is possible to combine two JL matrices by taking the so-called [[Khatri–Rao product#Face-splitting product|face-splitting product]], which is defined as the tensor products of the rows (was proposed by [[Vadym Slyusar|V. Slyusar]]<ref name= "Fortiana">{{citation
 | last1 = Esteve | first1 = Anna
 | last2 = Boj | first2 = Eva
 | last3 = Fortiana | first3 = Josep
 | doi = 10.1080/03610920802592860
 | issue = 18–20
 | journal = Communications in Statistics
 | mr = 2589790
 | pages = 3498–3509
 | title = Interaction terms in distance-based regression
 | volume = 38
 | year = 2009| s2cid = 122303508
 }}</ref> in 1996<ref name=slyusar>{{citation|last=Slyusar|first=V. I.|date= December 27, 1996|title=End products in matrices in radar applications. |url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/en/IZV_1998_3.pdf|journal=Radioelectronics and Communications Systems |volume=41 |issue=3|pages=50–53}}</ref><ref name=slyusar1>{{citation|last=Slyusar|first=V. I.|date=1997-05-20|title=Analytical model of the digital antenna array on a basis of face-splitting matrix products. |url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/ICATT97.pdf|journal=Proc. ICATT-97, Kyiv|pages=108–109}}</ref><ref name="DIPED">{{citation|last=Slyusar|first=V. I.|date=1997-09-15|title=New operations of matrices product for applications of radars|url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/DIPED_1997.pdf|journal=Proc. Direct and Inverse Problems of Electromagnetic and Acoustic Wave Theory (DIPED-97), Lviv.|pages=73–74}}</ref><ref name=slyusar2>{{citation|last=Slyusar|first=V. I.|date=March 13, 1998|title=A Family of Face Products of Matrices and its Properties|url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/FACE.pdf|journal=Cybernetics and Systems Analysis C/C of Kibernetika I Sistemnyi Analiz.- 1999.|volume=35|issue=3|pages=379–384|doi=10.1007/BF02733426|s2cid=119661450 }}</ref><ref name=general>{{citation|last=Slyusar|first=V. I.|date=2003|title=Generalized face-products of matrices in models of digital antenna arrays with nonidentical channels|url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/en/IZV_2003_10.pdf|journal=Radioelectronics and Communications Systems|volume=46|issue=10|pages=9–17}}</ref> for [[radar]] and [[digital antenna array]] applications).
More directly, let <math>{C}\in\mathbb R^{3\times 3}</math> and <math>{D}\in\mathbb R^{3\times 3}</math> be two matrices.
Then the [[Khatri–Rao product#Face-splitting product|face-splitting product]] <math>{C}\bullet {D}</math> is<ref name=slyusar /><ref name=slyusar1 /><ref name="DIPED" /><ref name=slyusar2 /><ref name=general />
:<math>
{C} \bullet {D}
= 
\left[
\begin{array} { c }
{C}_1 \otimes {D}_1\\\hline 
{C}_2 \otimes {D}_2\\\hline
{C}_3 \otimes {D}_3\\
\end{array}
\right].
</math>
This idea of tensorization was used by Kasiviswanathan et al. for [[differential privacy]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Kasiviswanathan | first1 = Shiva Prasad
 | last2 = Rudelson | first2 = Mark
 | last3 = Smith | first3 = Adam D.
 | last4 = Ullman | first4 = Jonathan R.
 | editor-last = Schulman | editor-first = Leonard J.
 | contribution = The price of privately releasing contingency tables and the spectra of random matrices with correlated rows
 | doi = 10.1145/1806689.1806795
 | pages = 775–784
 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery
 | title = Proceedings of the 42nd ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, STOC 2010, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA, 5–8 June 2010
 | year = 2010| osti = 990798
 | isbn = 978-1-4503-0050-6
 | s2cid = 5714334
 }}</ref>

JL matrices defined like this use fewer random bits, and can be applied quickly to vectors that have tensor structure, due to the following identity:<ref name="DIPED" />
:<math>(\mathbf{C} \bullet \mathbf{D})(x\otimes y) = \mathbf{C}x \circ \mathbf{D} y
= \left[
\begin{array} { c }
(\mathbf{C}x)_1 (\mathbf{D} y)_1 \\
(\mathbf{C}x)_2 (\mathbf{D} y)_2 \\
\vdots
\end{array}\right]
</math>,
where <math>\circ</math> is the element-wise ([[Hadamard product (matrices)|Hadamard]]) product.
Such computations have been used to efficiently compute [[polynomial kernel]]s and many other {{Clarify|date=June 2022|text=linear-algebra algorithms|reason=Terminology; we don't "compute" algorithms, but we run them. What do you mean by."}}.<ref name="woodruff">{{citation
 | last = Woodruff | first = David P.
 | arxiv = 1411.4357
 | doi = 10.1561/0400000060
 | series = Foundations and Trends in Theoretical Computer Science
 | mr = 3285427
 | title = Sketching as a Tool for Numerical Linear Algebra
 | volume = 10
 | year = 2014| s2cid = 51783444
 }}</ref>

In 2020<ref name="highdeg">{{citation
| contribution = Oblivious Sketching of High-Degree Polynomial Kernels
| first1 = Thomas
| last1 = Ahle
| first2 = Michael
| last2 = Kapralov
| first3 = Jakob
| last3 = Knudsen
| first4 = Rasmus
| last4 = Pagh | author4-link = Rasmus Pagh
| first5 = Ameya
| last5 = Velingker
| first6 = David
| last6 = Woodruff
| first7 = Amir
| last7 = Zandieh
| date = 2020
| publisher = Association for Computing Machinery
| title = ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms
| pages = 141–160
|doi = 10.1137/1.9781611975994.9| doi-access = free
| arxiv = 1909.01410
| isbn = 978-1-61197-599-4
}}</ref> it was shown that if the matrices <math>C_1, C_2, \dots, C_c</math> are independent <math>\pm1</math> or Gaussian matrices, the combined matrix <math>C_1 \bullet  \dots \bullet C_c</math> satisfies the distributional JL lemma if the number of rows is at least  
:<math>O(\epsilon^{-2}\log1/\delta + \epsilon^{-1}(\tfrac1c\log1/\delta)^c)</math>.

For large <math>\epsilon</math> this is as good as the completely random Johnson-Lindenstrauss, but
a matching lower bound in the same paper shows that this exponential dependency on <math>(\log1/\delta)^c</math> is necessary.
Alternative JL constructions are suggested to circumvent this.
